• Other names: Bluefin nothos, African annual killifish, Annual Killifish, Blueband killifish, Rainbow killifish
  • Water type: Freshwater
  • Tank size: 10 gallons (~40 litres)
  • Keeping: Easy
  • Breeding: Difficult
  • Size: 2.5–4.5 cm
  • Optimal temperature: 20–22°C
  • Optimal pH: 5.5–7.0
  • Optimal GH: 1–10
  • Dwellers: Middle-bottom
  • Nitrate: Less than 100
  • Diet: Omnivore
  • Temperament: Peaceful (with caution)
  • Life span: Up to 1 year
  • Colour form: Blue-orange

Interesting fact: These fish have become a well-established model for aging studies.

Nothobranchius rachovii is a small freshwater fish. The typical adult size is 2.5 to 4.5 cm. According to some studies, individuals have been reported reaching up to 8.0 cm; however, they were never seen growing that big in the aquarium.

  • Body shape. The body is long and laterally compressed, with a dorsal profile slightly concave on the head and convex from the nape to the end of the dorsal fin.
  • Head. Pointed snout and a terminal mouth slightly directed upward. The lower jaw protrudes forward. In the front row only a few teeth are larger, massive, conical and curved backward; behind this row all teeth are arranged in a wide row, and in the last row the teeth are not large.
  • Eyes. Medium-sized. The eye diameter is 3 1/3–3 1/2 times smaller than the head and 1 1/2 times smaller than the interorbital distance.
  • Coloration and pattern. Orange and black terminal stripes on the caudal fin. Males have alternating light blue and orange-red stripes on the body and fins, an orange-red head, and an orange subterminal and black terminal band in the caudal fin. The coloration, particularly on the head, may vary with aquarium conditions and water quality. Females are olive grey-brown; the frontal scales on the flanks are iridescent light blue to silvery. All fins are colorless.
  • Fins. 15–17 soft dorsal fin rays and 15–18 soft anal fin rays; no hard ray in the dorsal and anal fins. Pelvic fins are short, not reaching the origin of the anal fin; pectoral fins reach the origin of the pelvic fins. All unpaired fins are rounded.
  • Scales. 26 to 28.

Lifespan: Nothobranchius rachovii is an annual species. In the wild the average lifespan is 6–8 months; in aquariums with appropriate conditions, around 1 year. According to a study, maximum survival is about 15 months. In the last aging period the fish show spine curvature, loss of body coloration and progressive deterioration of the fins, especially the caudal fin. Aged fish (8 months) also showed reduced movement compared with young fish (3 months). Lifespan depends greatly on temperature; survival of 4-month-old fish was:

  • 90 days at 20°C,
  • 60 days at 25°C,
  • 33 days at 30°C.

The genus Nothobranchius consists of about 100 species. These are small fish, typically 4–7.5 cm standard length, with striking sexual dichromatism; males are brightly colored while females are mostly dull. Family: Nothobranchiidae; order: Cyprinodontiformes. The genus name derives from the Greek "nothos" (false) and "branchia" (gill). The species name honors the German aquarist Arthur Rachow (1884–1960), who donated a number of fish specimens to the Museum für Naturkunde.
This species is endemic to Mozambique. It inhabits the lower Zambezi and lower Pungwe River systems in Mozambique.

The natural habitats of Nothobranchius rachovii are seasonal pools and temporary water bodies where the water dries up annually.

Its life cycle is closely tied to the availability of water in these habitats produced by seasonal rains, and its rapid and short active life commences when rains fill the pool.

The recommended tank size is 10 gallons (40 litres) for 1 male and 2–3 females, which gives adequate space for swimming and hiding. For two breeding groups (2 males and 6 females), a 15-gallon (about 57 litres) aquarium is necessary, as the males establish and defend territories.

Important: Nothobranchius rachovii are good jumpers. To prevent this: use a lid, lower the water level, keep floating plants, and do not stress your fish.

Temperature: In the wild, about 20–24°C, but up to 30°C in the dry season. Since high temperatures significantly shorten lifespan, keep them at 20–22°C.

pH: 5.5–7.0.

Hardness: Recommended GH 1–10; KH 1–8. The species can adapt to harder water, but this also reduces its lifespan.

Water flow: In nature the fish live in shallow water with no or very slow current, so stagnant water or very slow currents are recommended. Experiments showed that Nothobranchius rachovii age faster under stress from continuous water recirculation.

Make sure the tank is properly cycled before adding the fish, and test water quality regularly with a kit.

Filtration: Filtration partly affects water flow, so choose filters with minimal flow, such as sponge filtration.

Lighting: They do not like bright light and prefer subdued lighting. If kept in planted tanks, adapt lighting to the plants' needs.

Substrate: No special requirements. A dark substrate makes the fish look more contrasting.

Plants and decorations: Plenty of dark hiding spots made of plants, rocks, stones, driftwood, coconuts, cork bark, leaves, PVC pipes and other decorations, which provide shelter and minimize stress, especially with several males. Some aquarists place items such as coconuts so that males use them as shelters and establish a central point from which to control their territory.

Stomach content analysis showed that Nothobranchius rachovii is a generalist, primarily consuming aquatic invertebrates (such as Cladocera, Copepoda, Ostracoda and Conchostraca) and mosquito larvae.

In aquariums they are easy to feed and not picky. They can be given a diverse range of frozen or live foods, including:

  • brine shrimp (Artemia salina),
  • Artemia nauplii,
  • daphnia,
  • fruit flies,
  • moina,
  • vinegar eels,
  • mosquito larvae,
  • cyclops,
  • detritus worms,
  • grindal worms,
  • bloodworms,
  • blackworms,
  • tubifex worms.

Large worms (grindal worms, bloodworms, blackworms, etc.) should be chopped into small pieces and flake food should be crumbled.

  • They are diurnal; feed them during the day.
  • Make sure the diet is mostly protein-based.
  • They are prone to overeating (follow the "5-minute rule").
  • Diet type: Omnivore; food preference: protein-rich; feeding frequency: daily.

Ideally feed twice a day (morning and evening).

Plant safe: Yes, they do not eat live plants. Planted tanks are highly recommended since they help reduce potential aggression.

Temper: Females are absolutely trouble-free, very peaceful and harmless. The species is mostly chosen for its brightly colored males, whose temperament matches their vibrant coloring. Besides aggression toward subordinate males, dominant males may also show aggression toward females and toward other fish species, even slightly larger ones. If there are several males in the aquarium, each will claim and guard its own territory.

Sociality: It is better to keep them in nest groups, with two to three females per male. To mitigate aggression, it is recommended to raise and breed them in groups of 5–6 males and 10–12 females without separating them. Isolating a male from the group, even for one week, can lead to problems. Keeping them in groups from the start distributes aggression evenly and offers a larger genetic pool, but requires larger aquariums.

Activity: This diurnal species is lively and active, constantly on the move, exploring with swift, agile movements, especially at feeding times. Interesting fact: Nothobranchius rachovii shows sleep-like states, with short periods of inactivity, floating near the surface with no pectoral fin movement during the night phase. Sleep is also identified when locomotor activity drops below the 33rd percentile.

Placement in tank: It spends most of its time in the open, often checking the bottom and hovering in midwater. It likes exploring and is fond of dense vegetation or hiding places.

  • Social: Yes
  • Activity: High
  • Placement: Middle and bottom dwellers
  • Peaceful: Conditionally
  • Nippers: No
  • Jumpers: Yes

Adult males are larger. Males and females are also easy to distinguish by color: males are much more colorful than drab females.

Interesting fact: Scientists noticed that removing males from a population leads to larger female fish that produce fewer eggs. They suggest that the absence of sexual stimuli reduces egg production, allowing females to save energy for growth.

Breeding is directly linked to the annual life cycle. In nature these fish inhabit water bodies that dry up completely, killing all the fish, so they lay eggs in mud so the next generation can be born and survive the drought until the rainy season. In aquariums this process has to be replicated completely.

Maturity: Depending on temperature, sexual maturity is reached from 3 weeks to 2 months of age.

Spawning: Spawning is portioned and prolonged, with several small batches of eggs laid daily. During courtship the male tries to press the female to the bottom; a distinctive feature is the male's "vertical" posture with the head upward. He makes sudden movements, often lowering his lower lip and holding his head at about 45°.

Fecundity: According to a study, females can lay 20–30 eggs per clutch per day at most; the average is typically 4–10.

Eggs: Fertilized eggs are adhesive, spherical, yellowish and demersal, with a large oil droplet. Their size is about 0.97±0.03 mm. The oil droplet serves as a food source. The egg envelope has two distinct layers that allow survival through dry periods.

Embryos: Embryos enter diapause for 6–9 months, with development slowing until the new rainy season. The eggs will not survive if fully submerged in water for more than a few weeks.

Fry: After hatching, fry grow and mature extremely fast. In nature nearly 90% of embryos and fry survive to adulthood. Average male length: 2.3 ± 0.15 cm at 1 month, 3.7 ± 0.22 cm at 4 months, 4.3 ± 0.35 cm at 7 months.

Breeding method:

  1. Put a male and a female into the breeding tank; provide peat or coconut fiber as substrate; condition them with lots of live food; raise the temperature to 25–26°C; lower the water level a bit.
  2. Tip: instead of adding the substrate directly into the aquarium, fill a small plastic jar with substrate (layer up to 2.5 cm). Some experienced aquarists recommend boiling peat for 3–5 minutes before use; this cleans the peat while preserving its acidic reaction. If boiled too long, almost all acids break down and the peat loses the ability to kill harmful bacteria that can destroy eggs spawned in the substrate.
  3. During spawning the female deposits eggs directly in the substrate and the male fertilizes them.
  4. After a few days of egg laying, return the breeders to the main tank; females, due to their very fast metabolism, often eat the eggs.
  5. If using a container with substrate, simply take it out of the water. Otherwise you must drain the aquarium completely to collect the substrate with eggs.
  6. Press the substrate slightly to remove excess water and let it dry. Important: dry it until it easily crumbles in your hands while still slightly moist. Overdrying can dehydrate the eggs and hinder development; insufficient drying can cause developmental delays.
  7. Place it in a plastic bag, sealed so that 3/4 is filled with air.
  8. Incubation usually lasts 6–9 months. Throughout, store the substrate at 21–25°C in a dark place. Once a month, air it and check the eggs. If the peat is too dry, moisten it.
  9. During incubation, monitor the development of the embryos' eyes; once they are formed, it is time to add water.
  10. Put the substrate back in the water. Keep the water soft (4–8 GH) and acidic (pH 6.0–6.5).
  11. Once the fry hatch, feed them infusoria. Make sure they always have food.

Eggs never develop all at once. This is a defense mechanism against so-called false rain, which allows the species to survive in nature, so fry hatch in batches.

Maintain water quality: regularly remove waste and leftovers. You can also add a few snails as a clean-up crew.

Ideally a species-only tank is recommended, given their relatively peaceful yet territorial nature.

Fish: If kept in community tanks, tank mates should be small species that cannot eat or harass them and that prefer (or tolerate) soft, slightly acidic water, such as neon tetras, Hemigrammus rhodostomus, brilliant rummynose tetra, least killifish (Heterandria formosa), pencilfish, harlequin rasboras, pygmy cory, etc.

Shrimp: They can be kept with dwarf shrimp to some degree. They are not a threat to adult or even juvenile shrimp, but newly hatched shrimp (about 2 mm) fit in their mouth and will be eaten from time to time.

Snails: Compatible with any freshwater snail.

Avoid: large and/or aggressive and/or boisterous fish; all types of crayfish and most freshwater crabs.

Conclusion: Nothobranchius rachovii is a fascinating and beautiful aquarium fish, relatively easy to care for in a species tank and suitable for beginners, but the males' territorial behavior and the challenges of breeding must always be kept in mind.
